video_title: How to Build the Next SpaceX or Tesla
gist: Despite the 'next SpaceX or Tesla' title, this is mainly a16z American Dynamism partners Connor and Aaron discussing the AD50 list (inputs, factories, systems). They argue that defense spending subsidizes a dual-use US industrial base that will enable robotics, that a co-engineering 'manufacturing middle' of suppliers is emerging, and that risk capital in defense in H1 2026 exceeded all of 2025.

themes.theme: Defense as subsidizer of the industrial base

insights.claim: a16z's AD50 list this year is organized into three pillars, inputs (minerals out of the ground), factories and end systems, because American Dynamism companies need to be evaluated across the whole value chain.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Investment opportunity spans the whole supply chain, not just defense primes and end-system makers.

insights.claim: Defense buyers can act as the first customer that subsidizes heavy capex (for example a new US PCB fab), and the same capacity then serves robots, hearing aids and other commercial markets.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Defense contracts reduce the risk of capex for companies whose real markets are dual-use.
insights.quote: you know what else has PCB boards? Robots.

insights.claim: DJI shows the path from consumer drones to high-volume defense drone production to becoming the world's largest robot producer, because a drone motor is very similar to a robot actuator, the hardest part of building a robot.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: The US needs a domestic equivalent; drone and defense subsystem makers are a lead-in to robotics.
insights.quote: what is very similar to a drone motor is a robot actuator

insights.claim: The actuators, motors, valves and switches built for military autonomous systems from Saronic, Anduril and Castelion are the same subsystems future robots need, so the defense build-out will enable a US robotics wave without relying on Chinese factories.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: The defense component supply chain is upstream of US robotics.

insights.claim: A robotics company deploying today has a '99% chance' that most of what it buys comes from China.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: There is a large onshoring opportunity in robotics components.
insights.quote: there's a 99% chance that majority of what they are buying is coming from China

insights.claim: SpaceX and Tesla vertically integrated because there was no US industrial base (for example no battery supply chain) to support them; startups should use high-quality suppliers where they exist and integrate only for exquisite systems or missing supply chains.
insights.speaker: Connor / Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: How much a company vertically integrates should depend on how mature its suppliers are.

insights.claim: Mariana Minerals bought a copper mine and runs the whole value chain (acquire, develop, mine, operate, refine) because incumbent miners would not adopt technology fast enough; owning the asset lets it capture the data and the value of its technology.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: In the physical world, owning the asset may be needed to capture the value of the technology.

insights.claim: Factory software makers such as Hadrian win through 15-20 incremental process improvements across quoting, machining, inspection and handling, not one AI silver bullet; 'AI cannot turn a wrench yet.'
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Physical-world AI value comes from deep process knowledge, not from simply adding models.
insights.quote: AI cannot turn a wrench yet.

insights.claim: AI tools let manufacturing technicians reconfigure high-mix, low-volume lines themselves, for example by using Claude in about 20 minutes, instead of paying a systems integrator hundreds of thousands of dollars over about 3 months.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: This changes US manufacturing economics in favor of the high-mix production it relies on.

insights.claim: A portfolio company used to order twice the PCBs it needed because about 50% failed quality tests; with new US PCB startups as suppliers, 70-90% now pass.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Domestic suppliers that work closely with customers can beat offshore suppliers on quality, not only on geopolitics.

insights.claim: Private venture capital lets defense startups build ahead of formal government requirements (for example, Castelion's hypersonic missile was venture-funded for about 3 years before contracts), so neo-primes will take market share from legacy primes.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: There is structural share shift from primes to venture-backed defense companies.

insights.claim: Anduril's facilities in Ohio and Baltimore and Saronic's shipyard are set to produce thousands to hundreds of thousands of systems, which is scale the US has not achieved in a long time.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Defense tech is moving from prototypes to rate production.

insights.claim: Legacy tier suppliers like Honeywell have been in 'receive mode' for 40 years, reusing decades-old designs such as 737 landing gear; new end systems will need a 'manufacturing middle' that co-engineers subcomponents with OEMs, creating an 'American manufacturing asset class'.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Sub-tier suppliers that co-engineer with OEMs are an underappreciated venture category.
insights.quote: we're creating the American manufacturing asset class right now

insights.claim: The grid is shifting from static mechanical systems deployed in the 1970s-80s to software-native power electronics and battery storage, which opens the entire supply chain to redesign.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Power-electronics and grid-hardware startups benefit from the architecture reset.

insights.claim: Even if only half of the projected demand (for example, a fourfold increase in energy) materializes, demand for redesigned components does not reverse, because better cost, serviceability and manufacturability mean buyers never go back.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: The thesis holds even if demand forecasts are too high.

insights.claim: Founders and engineers who leave Anduril, SpaceX, Tesla or Saronic after solving internal supply-chain problems start supplier companies with a ready, sympathetic customer base, repeating how the Silicon Valley/YC ecosystem was built.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Alumni networks are a sourcing edge for supplier startups.

insights.claim: Hardware companies now make up the majority of the world's 10 most valuable companies, and Palantir, Anduril and SpaceX show that defense and industrial companies can be among the largest businesses.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: The pool of ambitious founders entering hard tech is growing.
insights.quote: 10 most valuable companies in the world, like the majority of them are hardware companies.

insights.claim: More risk capital went into the defense ecosystem in the first half of 2026 than in all of 2025, which was itself many times more than the year before; the 'valley of death' is starting to disappear.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Funding conditions for defense tech are at a cyclical high, so watch for crowding.
insights.quote: the first half of 2026, more uh more risk dollars went into the defense ecosystem than all of last year combined

insights.claim: JPMorgan has committed very large sums to physical-world investment, and private equity and large credit firms are now entering American Dynamism categories in a big way.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Non-venture capital is arriving to fund capital-intensive scale-up.

insights.claim: The US lacks top-down industrial policy like China's, which Connor sees as an advantage because private capital follows success and can fund ahead of obvious demand.
insights.speaker: Connor (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Expect a market-driven, uneven US build-out rather than state-directed allocation.

insights.claim: The US's flat power-production curve versus China's steep rise is not a technology problem but a question of national will to permit and build.
insights.speaker: Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Permitting and politics, not technology, set the pace of US energy build-out.
insights.quote: I don't think that that is a um technology problem.

insights.claim: Physical-world companies take years to build, and capital markets need patience; physical projects also need community buy-in, and Amco is cited as partnering with small machine shops instead of cutting staff.
insights.speaker: Connor / Aaron (a16z American Dynamism)
insights.so_what: Local opposition and long timelines are the main execution risks.
